prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The monocular depth map captures the large-scale outdoor layout of the baseball field, showing a continuous brightness gradient along the ground from bright white grass immediately in front of the camera wearer (1 to 3 metres away, with no objects or people within arm's reach) to mid-grey across the dirt infield (15 to 45 metres away) and dark grey along the backstop, covered dugout/bleachers to the right-center, tall light poles, and background tree line (50 to 100+ metres away), with the sky in black above. Across the 5 frames, the bright foreground band tilts upward on the left in frame 2 and levels out through frames 3 to 5, reflecting the camera wearer's head roll and slight forward progression toward the infield. Compared to the RGB strip alone, the depth map makes the ground plane slope and the silhouettes of the thin vertical light poles and distant tree canopy stand out clearly against the sky. However, the map is unreliable for small distant entities: the tiny people standing on the infield (roughly 25 to 40 metres away and 10 to 20 metres apart) are completely absorbed into the surrounding ground depth, so their positions, facing directions, and any mutual occlusions cannot be read from depth.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map is almost entirely blank across all 5 frames, providing no spatial masks for the baseball diamond, the covered bleachers and fences 50 to 70 metres ahead, or the distant people standing on the infield 25 to 40 metres in front of the camera wearer. Nothing is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or visibly held by others in the RGB view, and the segmentation map detects no foreground or background objects as the camera tilts in frame 2 and levels out in frames 3 to 5. Its only output is a tiny false-positive mask labeled 'k' (a truncated class label) high on the far-right edge of frame 1 where a light pole top is partly cut off by the frame border, which vanishes in frames 2 through 5. Consequently, the segmentation map adds no useful spatial information beyond the RGB image and is unreliable at this wide-angle, long-range scale because it misses every person and structure while hallucinating an object on the light pole.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is completely black across all 5 frames, containing zero body or hand skeletons anywhere in the scene. While the RGB strip shows tiny figures on the dirt infield roughly 25 to 40 metres in front of the camera wearer (and 10 to 20 metres from one another) with no body parts of the camera wearer or other objects within arm's reach, those distant people occupy too few pixels for keypoint detection. Because no skeletons are rendered, the map cannot indicate which way the distant people face, whether they look toward the camera wearer, whether their limbs are occluded, or how their poses change across the 5 frames. The pose map therefore offers no spatial detail beyond confirming the absence of near-field bodies or hands in view, and is entirely unreliable for tracking people at long outdoor distances.
